s0003.literal: Prince Xian of Hengyang Chen Chang; Prince Min of Nankang Chen Tanlang; sons Fangtai and Fangqing
s0003.idiomatic: Prince Xian of Hengyang Chen Chang; Prince Min of Nankang Chen Tanlang; sons Fangtai and Fangqing

s0004.literal: Prince Xian of Hengyang Chen Chang
s0004.idiomatic: Prince Xian of Hengyang Chen Chang

s0005.literal: Prince Xian of Hengyang Chen Chang, courtesy name Jingye, was the Founder's sixth son.
s0005.idiomatic: Chen Chang, Prince Xian of Hengyang, styled Jingye, was the Founder's sixth son.

s0006.literal: At the end of Liang's Taiping era, the Founder campaigned south against Li Bin and ordered Chang and Lady Xuan to return to Wuxing with Shen Ke.
s0006.idiomatic: In the last years of Liang's Taiping era, the Founder marched south against Li Bin and sent Chang and Lady Xuan back to Wuxing with Shen Ke.

s0007.literal: When the Founder marched east against Hou Jing, Chang, Lady Xuan, and Emperor Wen were all imprisoned by Jing.
s0007.idiomatic: When the Founder turned east against Hou Jing, Chang, Lady Xuan, and Emperor Wen were all taken prisoner by Jing.

s0008.literal: When Jing was suppressed, Chang was appointed Heir of the Princedom of Changcheng and Administrator of Wuxing, aged sixteen.
s0008.idiomatic: After Jing's defeat he was made heir of the princedom of Changcheng and administrator of Wuxing, at age sixteen.

s0009.literal: Chang's appearance was grand and handsome, his bearing bright and open; by nature he was clever and eloquent and well versed in administration.
s0009.idiomatic: Chang was tall and handsome, with a clear, spirited face; he was quick-witted and articulate and knew government affairs well.

s0010.literal: The Founder sent Xie Zhe of Chen commandery and Cai Jingli of Jiyang to assist Chang in the commandery, and Du Zhiwei of Wu commandery to instruct him in the classics.
s0010.idiomatic: The Founder sent Xie Zhe of Chen and Cai Jingli of Jiyang to help him govern the commandery, and Du Zhiwei of Wu to teach him the classics.

s0011.literal: Chang read a text once and could recite it; he understood principles clearly and reasoned with fluent penetration.
s0011.idiomatic: He could read a passage once and recite it from memory, grasp doctrine clearly, and argue through a point without hesitation.

s0012.literal: Soon he went to Jingzhou with Emperor Xuan; Emperor Yuan of Liang appointed him External Regular Attendant of the Secretariat.
s0012.idiomatic: He soon went to Jingzhou with Emperor Xuan; Emperor Yuan of Liang made him external regular attendant of the Secretariat.

s0013.literal: When Jingzhou fell, he again moved with Emperor Xuan to the region west of the Pass; Western Wei treated him with great honor on the Founder's account.
s0013.idiomatic: When Jingzhou fell he was moved with Emperor Xuan to the northwest; Western Wei honored him greatly for the Founder's sake.

s0014.literal: Your servant has heard that imperial sons shore up the realm—the glorious standard of elevated Zhou—and that enfeoffed domains as screens was Han's grand rule; thus the dynasty's endurance truly relied on Xing and Wei, [1] and the sacred mandate's longevity truly depended on the lands of the He and Chu.
s0014.idiomatic: We have heard that kinsmen of the royal house buttress the state, as in glorious Zhou, and that enfeoffing princes to guard the borders was Han's great design; lasting rule truly drew on domains such as Xing and Wei, [1] and the mandate's endurance truly rested on great regions such as the He River lands and Chu.

s0015.literal: We bow that Your Majesty's divine counsel shines broad, sacred virtue revered and bright, the Way towers above sun and moon, and virtue matches creation.
s0015.idiomatic: Your Majesty's divine plan shines far; your sacred virtue is revered and clear; your Way rises above sun and moon; your virtue equals heaven and earth.

s0016.literal: In the past, when the royal enterprise had only begun and Heaven's course was still hard, you took part in counsel and joined righteous heroes; your martial prestige was shown abroad and divine might settled within—thus you twice restored Yu's traces and greatly sheltered the living people.
s0016.idiomatic: When the throne was first being won and the realm was still in peril, you shared in strategy and rallied men of honor; your power reached beyond the borders and your strength secured the court—so you twice restored the ancient order and sheltered the people.

s0017.literal: When the Sage Martial ascended far away, the royal army halted in the distance; the imperial heir was cut off afar and succession had no home; the ancestral temple was in peril and the jade beads hung loose beyond compare.
s0017.idiomatic: When the sage martial emperor passed away, the royal army was far away; the heir was cut off and the succession unsettled; the ancestral temple trembled and the throne seemed all but lost.

s0018.literal: Then the relay carriage announced return, the ministers fixed the plan, you took our great foundation, and the bright fortune shone forth; the people's hearts had a lord, the imperial tombs were secure, and renewal came on this day—human feeling and Heaven's intent were plainly to be sought.
s0018.idiomatic: Then word came that the heir was returning, the ministers settled the succession, you took up the great foundation, and the bright age began; the people had a ruler, the tombs were safe, and renewal came on that day—men's hearts and Heaven's will alike were clear.

s0019.literal: Wang Lin defied the mandate and long evaded punishment; now he has joined with dogs and sheep, riding the current to loose calamity—boats and banners in wild array, the river covered and the land hidden; troops weary and the people spent, the loom shuttles empty; within and without in turmoil, the frontier screens had no hold.
s0019.idiomatic: Wang Lin had long rebelled and escaped justice; now he joined with barbarian allies and struck along the rivers—fleets and banners filled the land, the Yangzi hidden and the shores covered; armies were exhausted, the people drained, and the realm was in uproar while the borders gave way.

s0020.literal: You then ate late at court and issued orders upon the current; the azure rhinoceros banner had already galloped forth and the long serpent cut itself down; the four quarters were cleared and the eight cords washed clean; your great design was raised afar and benevolent fame carried far; where virtue and transformation reached, the wind blew and grass bent—thus your merit was deeper than slight Yu's and your Way greater than sole Yao's; how could it be only the altars of soil and grain that were settled? The black-haired people likewise relied on you.
s0020.idiomatic: You labored at court and sent armies down the rivers; once your forces moved, the rebel host collapsed; you cleared the four quarters and pacified the realm, your design reaching far and your kindness heard abroad; where your rule reached, men yielded like grass in wind—your merit outshone the saviors of old and your Way surpassed the sage kings; it was not only the state that was saved—the people leaned on you.

s0021.literal: The sixth imperial younger brother Chang, recently sent as hostage in his prime years, fell into the enemy's grasp, cut off beyond the frontier passes, unable to return in a turn of the heel.
s0021.idiomatic: Your sixth brother Chang was sent north as a hostage while still young; he fell into enemy hands and was cut off beyond the passes, unable to come home.

s0022.literal: Your Majesty's love within the heavenly bonds is already deep, and your constant thought is yielding virtue.
s0022.idiomatic: Your love for your kin runs deep, and you have long wished to yield your own desire.

s0023.literal: We submit that great virtue is without selfishness and supreme fairness is ever present—how can one indulge a common man's constant feelings and forget the royal enterprise's great plan?
s0023.idiomatic: Great virtue knows no private favor, and supreme justice must prevail—how can private feeling outweigh the needs of the throne?

s0024.literal: Take the old precedents as law, follow the ritual canon in form, emulate Zhou and Han, and establish worthy kin.
s0024.idiomatic: Follow ancient precedent, observe the rites, and as Zhou and Han did, enfeoff worthy kinsmen.

s0025.literal: The Xiang region's terrain is strategically vital and commands rivers and hills; the charge of guarding the wall none but kin should hold; he should open his fief at Heng and Yi and likewise receive lofty insignia.
s0025.idiomatic: Xiang province is a strategic land of rivers and hills; only a kinsman should hold its defense; let him take Hengyang and receive the honors due a prince.

s0026.literal: We your servants jointly propose that Chang be made Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Area Commander over Military Affairs in Xiangzhou, General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Xiangzhou; that he be enfeoffed as Prince of Hengyang commandery with a fief of five thousand households; and that there be added a black-wheeled carriage with three canopy poles, a rear guard of drums and pipes, and twenty halberd-bearers.
s0026.idiomatic: We propose that Chang be made bearer of the staff, palace attendant, commander of armies in Xiangzhou, general of agile cavalry, and governor of Xiangzhou; that he be enfeoffed as Prince of Hengyang with five thousand households; and that he receive a black carriage with triple canopy, a guard of drums and pipes, and twenty halberd escorts.

s0027.idiomatic: Let this memorial be carried out.

s0029.literal: In the third month he entered the realm; an edict ordered Secretariat clerks to welcome him along the route.
s0029.idiomatic: In the third month he crossed the border; the throne ordered secretariat clerks to meet him all along the road.

s0030.literal: On jingzi day he crossed the river; midstream his boat broke and he died by drowning.
s0030.idiomatic: On jingzi day he crossed the Yangzi; midstream the boat broke up and he drowned.

s0031.literal: On gengyin day of the fourth month the bier reached the capital; the emperor went out in person to mourn and weep.
s0031.idiomatic: On gengyin day in the fourth month the coffin reached the capital; the emperor went out in person to mourn.

s0032.literal: Then an edict was issued: "Favor and insignia are meant to honor virtue, and ritual is meant to exalt kin—these are the constant rules of successive ages and the fixed statutes of former kings.
s0032.idiomatic: An edict followed: "Honors reward virtue, and ritual exalts kin—this has been the rule of every age and the law of former kings.

s0033.literal: The newly appointed Bearer of the Staff, Palace Attendant, Area Commander over Military Affairs in Xiangzhou, General of Agile Cavalry, and Governor of Xiangzhou, Prince of Hengyang Chen Chang, had wisdom present in his person and jade and regalia early in bloom; filial reverence steeped within, keen insight shown without.
s0033.idiomatic: Chen Chang, newly made bearer of the staff, palace attendant, commander of armies in Xiangzhou, general of agile cavalry, and governor of Xiangzhou, Prince of Hengyang, was wise in himself and gifted from youth, inwardly filial and outwardly sharp.

s0034.literal: In Liang's years of hardship the altars toppled; the western capital was lost and he was trapped in the passes of Guan and Long.
s0034.idiomatic: In Liang's troubled years the dynasty fell; the western capital was lost and he was held captive in the northwest.

s0035.literal: When the great enterprise was first founded, outer regions defied the mandate; envoys were blocked and messages could not pass; we looked on that distant bridge, nearly bordering the crows of dusk.
s0035.idiomatic: When the Chen house first rose, the frontiers were closed to us; no envoy could reach him and no word come through; we thought of him far away, almost beyond return.

s0036.literal: Now the ministers have joined their strength and many hardships are cleared; light carriages enter the walls without need to borrow a road.
s0036.idiomatic: Now that the ministers have joined their strength and the realm is pacified, he could come home without asking leave of any foe.

s0037.literal: The Zhou court honored renewed kinship and the paired horses returned; we rejoice at this morning's news and hope for the evening's comfort of his presence.
s0037.idiomatic: Zhou once welcomed a kinsman home from captivity; we rejoiced to hear he was coming and hoped at last to see him again.

s0038.literal: Repayment of kindness was only words—he never aided our virtue; when a man is gone, the wasting grief is here; suddenly he died and our mourning redoubled.
s0038.idiomatic: Heaven repaid him only with words, not with years; now he is gone and our grief is doubled.

s0039.literal: The grief at the ford gate is empty; the longing for Mount Heng cannot be pursued; speaking of it in silence, the heart is as if cut apart.
s0039.idiomatic: We grieve at the river where he died, but cannot follow him to his grave; to think of it is to feel the heart torn.

s0040.literal: Grand honors should be raised to match his bright merit.
s0040.idiomatic: Let great honors be granted to match his worth.

s0041.literal: He may be posthumously made Palace Attendant, given the yellow battle-axe, made Area Commander over All Military Affairs within and without, Grand Tutor, and Governor of Yangzhou.
s0041.idiomatic: Posthumously appoint him palace attendant, grant the yellow battle-axe, make him commander of all armies at court and in the field, grand tutor, and governor of Yangzhou.

s0042.literal: Grant the warm-bright secret vessels of the Eastern Garden, the nine tassels and imperial carriage, the yellow canopy and left banner, a hundred tiger-guard halberd-bearers, [2] the encoffining carriage, and front and rear guards with feather fans, drums, and pipes.
s0042.idiomatic: Grant the Eastern Garden burial regalia, the nine-tasseled carriage and imperial equipage, a hundred halberd guards, [2] the funeral carriage, and front and rear guards with drums and pipes.

s0043.literal: The rites of burial and escort shall wholly follow the precedents of the Han Prince Xian of Dongping and the Qi Prince Wen of Yuzhang.
s0043.idiomatic: Burial and escort shall follow the precedents of the Han Prince Xian of Dongping and the Qi Prince Wen of Yuzhang.

s0044.literal: Still dispatch the Grand Minister of Works, bearer of the staff, to meet and escort the funeral; the Grand Herald shall assist with the guard of feathers; whatever the bier and escort require shall be fully provided along the way.
s0044.idiomatic: Send the grand minister of works with the staff to receive the coffin; let the grand herald assist with the guard; provide everything needed for the funeral along the route.

s0046.literal: He had no sons; Emperor Wen made his seventh son Boxin heir.
s0046.idiomatic: He left no sons; Emperor Wen made his seventh son Boxin his heir.

s0047.literal: Prince Min of Nankang Chen Tanlang
s0047.idiomatic: Prince Min of Nankang Chen Tanlang

s0048.literal: Prince Min of Nankang Chen Tanlang was the son of Prince Zhongzhuang Xiuxian, younger brother of the Founder's mother.
s0048.idiomatic: Chen Tanlang, Prince Min of Nankang, was the son of Prince Zhongzhuang Xiuxian, the Founder's maternal uncle.

s0049.literal: Xiuxian in youth was bold and free with great ambition; when Emperor Jianwen of Liang was in the eastern palace he was deeply favored.
s0049.idiomatic: Xiuxian was daring and ambitious in youth; when Emperor Jianwen of Liang was crown prince he won deep favor.

s0050.literal: In Taqing, after welcoming Hou Jing, with affairs in the north he had Xiuxian recruit over a thousand men and appointed him Commander of Wende; soon he died.
s0050.idiomatic: In the Taqing era, after Hou Jing was admitted and war moved north, he had Xiuxian raise more than a thousand men and made him commander of Wende; he died soon after.

s0051.literal: When the Founder had the realm, he often said of Xiuxian: "If this younger brother had lived, settling the Yellow and Luo would not have been hard.
s0051.idiomatic: Once the Founder held the realm, he often said of Xiuxian: "If this brother had lived, the Yellow and Luo would not have been hard to recover.

s0052.literal: " When Emperor Jing of Liang took the throne, he was posthumously made Palace Attendant, Bearer of the Staff, General of Agile Cavalry, and Inspector of South Xuzhou, and enfeoffed as Duke of Wukang county with a fief of one thousand households.
s0052.idiomatic: " When Emperor Jing of Liang came to the throne, Xiuxian was posthumously made palace attendant, bearer of the staff, general of agile cavalry, and inspector of South Xuzhou, and enfeoffed as Duke of Wukang with one thousand households.

s0053.literal: When the Founder accepted the abdication, he was posthumously made Palace Attendant, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Grand Tutor, enfeoffed as Prince of Nankang commandery with two thousand households, posthumous name Zhongzhuang.
s0053.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, he was posthumously made palace attendant, grand general of chariots and cavalry, and grand tutor, enfeoffed as Prince of Nankang with two thousand households, and given the posthumous name Zhongzhuang.

s0054.literal: In year two, Xu Siwei and Ren Yue led Qi invaders to press the capital; they soon sued for peace and asked for the Founder's sons and nephews as hostages.
s0054.idiomatic: In year two, Xu Siwei and Ren Yue brought Qi armies against the capital; they then sought peace and demanded the Founder's sons and nephews as hostages.

s0055.literal: At the time many commanderies and districts had not yet submitted, the capital was weak, and grain transport was cut off; civil and military officials at court all wished to make peace with Qi, and the Founder found it hard—but he also could not lightly go against the assembly; he then spoke in court, saying: "I wrongly aided the royal house and let barbarians run riot in Xia, unable to destroy them—where can I escape blame?
s0055.idiomatic: Many provinces had not yet submitted, the capital was weak, and supplies were failing; court officials all favored peace with Qi, and the Founder was torn—but he could not easily defy them. He told the assembly: "I have poorly served the dynasty and let barbarians ravage the realm without destroying them—how can I escape blame?

s0056.literal: Now the worthies in office wish to rest shoulders and lay down arms, make peace with Qi, and quiet the frontier; if I go against the assembly, they will surely say I spare my sons and nephews—today I resolve to send Tanlang and abandon him in the enemy court.
s0056.idiomatic: You wish to rest and make peace with Qi to quiet the borders; if I refuse, you will say I spare my kin—today I will send Tanlang and abandon him to the enemy.

s0057.literal: Moreover the Qi are faithless and their coveting does not cease; seeing us weaken day by day, they will surely break the pact.
s0057.idiomatic: The Qi are faithless and will not stop their scheming; seeing us weaken, they will surely break the treaty.

s0058.literal: If Qi invaders come, you gentlemen must fight hard for me."
s0058.idiomatic: If the Qi attack again, you must fight for me with all your strength."

s0059.literal: The Founder feared Tanlang would dread the journey or flee east along the road; he himself led foot and horse to Jingkou to meet him, brought Tanlang back to the capital, and then sent him as hostage to Qi.
s0059.idiomatic: The Founder feared Tanlang would refuse or flee east; he went in person with troops to Jingkou to fetch him, brought him back to the capital, and then sent him to Qi as a hostage.

s0060.literal: Qi indeed broke the pact and again sent Xiao Gui and others to follow Siwei across the river; the Founder fought them and inflicted a great defeat, capturing Xiao Gui, Dongfang Lao, and others.
s0060.idiomatic: Qi broke the treaty and sent Xiao Gui and others with Siwei across the Yangzi; the Founder defeated them heavily and took Xiao Gui, Dongfang Lao, and others prisoner.

s0061.literal: The Qi asked to cede territory and present horses and cattle to ransom them; the Founder would not agree.
s0061.idiomatic: Qi offered to cede land and send horses and cattle as ransom; the Founder refused.

s0062.literal: When Gui and the others were executed, the Qi also killed Tanlang at Jinyang; at the time [year] twenty-eight.
s0062.idiomatic: When Gui and the rest were put to death, the northerners also killed Tanlang at Jinyang; he was twenty-eight. (The text supplies the missing word "year".)

s0063.literal: Editorial footnote marker 3. At the time, already broken with Qi, they did not know of it.
s0063.idiomatic: Editorial footnote marker 3. The court had already broken with Qi and did not yet know.

s0064.literal: When the Founder took the throne, he still had Tanlang succeed as Prince of Nankang commandery to maintain the sacrifices to Prince Zhongzhuang, his ritual rank the same as an imperial prince.
s0064.idiomatic: When the Founder became emperor, he still had Tanlang recorded as Prince of Nankang to maintain Prince Zhongzhuang's sacrifices, with honors equal to an imperial prince.

s0065.literal: In the second year of Tiankang, when Qi made peace, they first learned of it.
s0065.idiomatic: In Tiankang year two, when peace was made with Qi, the court first learned he was dead.

s0066.literal: Emperor Wen issued an edict: "To honor the distant dead and be careful in the final rites—this we have heard in former instructions.
s0066.idiomatic: Emperor Wen issued an edict: "To honor the dead and observe the last rites is an ancient teaching.

s0067.literal: Prince of Nankang Chen Tanlang, wise and bright in his kinship, was the pillar of the frontier screens; he went as hostage to Northern Qi to ease the time's hardship.
s0067.idiomatic: Prince of Nankang Chen Tanlang was a worthy kinsman and a pillar of the realm; he went as hostage to Northern Qi to ease the crisis.

s0068.literal: The imperial fortune was just rising and he did not yet return; we long looked for him day and night without forgetting.
s0068.idiomatic: The dynasty was rising and he had not returned; we longed for him day and night.

s0069.literal: When Qi's envoys first arrived, the grievous news came suddenly; in recalling him our grief doubled beyond the common measure; grand favor should be raised to brighten the constant order.
s0069.idiomatic: When Qi's envoys first came, word of his death arrived; our grief was beyond measure; let honors be raised to mark his place.

s0070.literal: He may be posthumously made Palace Attendant, General Who Pacifies the East, Opener of the Mansion Equal to the Three Dukes, and Inspector of South Xuzhou; posthumous title Min.
s0070.idiomatic: Posthumously appoint him palace attendant, general who pacifies the east, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and inspector of South Xuzhou; posthumous title Min.

s0071.literal: " Then he dispatched the acting director of the palace secretariat, together with the envoys on the mission, Jiang Dezao and Liu Shizhi, to meet Tanlang's bier; in spring of year three it reached the capital.
s0071.idiomatic: " He sent the acting director of the palace secretariat, Jiang Dezao and Liu Shizhi, with the embassy to bring Tanlang's coffin home; it reached the capital in spring of year three.

s0072.literal: Earlier, before Tanlang was hostage in Qi, he had sons Fangtai and Fangqing.
s0072.idiomatic: Before Tanlang went to Qi as a hostage, he had sons Fangtai and Fangqing.

s0073.literal: When he was about to go to Qi, he took two concubines with him; in the north he also had two more sons—Fanghua and Fangkuang—who likewise returned.
s0073.idiomatic: When he was sent to Qi he took two concubines; in the north he fathered two more sons, Fanghua and Fangkuang, who also came back.

s0075.literal: Fangtai in youth was rough and reckless; he gathered with wicked young men and roamed without limit; because of the Prince of Nankang, Emperor Wen especially indulged him.
s0075.idiomatic: Fangtai was coarse and unruly from youth, running with bad company and living without restraint; because of his grandfather the prince, Emperor Wen especially spared him.

s0076.literal: In the first year of Tiankang, an edict said: "Prince of Nankang Chen Tanlang, cut off in the Qi court, his return uncertain; the state temple is being restored and sacrifices need a master—his eldest son Fangtai may be made Heir of Nankang and succeed the Prince of Nankang."
s0076.idiomatic: In Tiankang year one an edict said: "Prince of Nankang Chen Tanlang is held in Qi and cannot return; the ancestral temple is being restored and needs a master—let his eldest son Fangtai be heir of Nankang and succeed the title."

s0077.literal: Later they heard Tanlang had died; thereupon he succeeded to the title of Prince of Nankang.
s0077.idiomatic: When word came that Tanlang had died, Fangtai succeeded as Prince of Nankang.

s0078.literal: Soon he was made General of Benevolent Might and Administrator of Danyang, with staff officers appointed.
s0078.idiomatic: He was soon made general of benevolent might and administrator of Danyang, with a full staff.

s0079.literal: In the fourth year of Taijian he was transferred to Bearer of the Staff and Area Commander over Military Affairs in the nineteen provinces of Guang, Heng, Jiao, Yue, Cheng, Ding, Ming, Xin, He, Luo, De, Yi, Huang, Li, An, Jian, Shiya, and others, [4] General Who Pacifies the Yue, and Inspector of Guangzhou.
s0079.idiomatic: In Taijian year four he was made bearer of the staff and commander of armies in nineteen southern provinces including Guang, Heng, Jiao, Yue, Cheng, Ding, Ming, Xin, He, Luo, De, Yi, Huang, Li, An, Jian, and Shiya, [4] general who pacifies the Yue, and inspector of Guangzhou.

s0080.literal: His government was cruel and violent; the responsible offices memorialized against him and he was removed from office.
s0080.idiomatic: He governed with cruelty; the authorities reported him and he was dismissed.

s0081.literal: Soon he was reappointed General of Benevolent Might, with staff officers appointed.
s0081.idiomatic: He was soon restored as general of benevolent might with a staff.

s0082.literal: In year six he was given the staff and made Area Commander over Military Affairs in Yuzhang commandery and Interior Magistrate of Yuzhang.
s0082.idiomatic: In year six he received the staff and was made commander of armies in Yuzhang and interior magistrate of the commandery.

s0083.literal: In the commandery he did not attend to the people's affairs; as his term neared its end he repeatedly sent his retainers out to rob, and also set fires that spread through the towns, then went about violent plunder, seizing and registering the rich and extorting wealth.
s0083.idiomatic: In office he neglected the people; as his term ended he sent retainers to rob, set fires that burned towns, and plundered openly, seizing the wealthy and extorting bribes.

s0084.literal: When his replacement arrived, he still detained himself and would not return.
s0084.idiomatic: When his successor arrived he lingered and would not leave.

s0085.literal: On reaching the capital, an edict made him Director of the Imperial Clan, his general's title and staff unchanged.
s0085.idiomatic: At the capital an edict made him director of the imperial clan, keeping his general's rank and staff.

s0086.literal: Before he took up the post, he was impeached by the censor-in-chief Zong Yuanrao, removed from office, and sent to his princely residence as a prince only.
s0086.idiomatic: Before he took office the censor-in-chief Zong Yuanrao impeached him; he was dismissed and sent back to his princely residence.

s0087.literal: In year eleven he was reappointed General Who Pacifies the Distance and assigned to the Direct Palace Office.
s0087.idiomatic: In year eleven he was made general who pacifies the distance and posted to the Direct Palace Office.

s0088.literal: Soon he was additionally made Regular Attendant of the Secretariat, with staff appointed as needed.
s0088.idiomatic: He was soon also made regular attendant of the Secretariat, with staff as required.

s0089.literal: In the eighth month of that year Emperor Xuan visited the Great Zhuang Hall and there held a great review of troops, ordering Area Commander Ren Zhong to lead one hundred thousand foot and horse arrayed at Xuanwu Lake, and Area Commander Chen Jing to lead five hundred tower ships out on the Guazhou stretch of the Yangzi; Emperor Xuan ascended the Xuanwu Gate tower [5] and feasted the ministers to watch.
s0089.idiomatic: That eighth month Emperor Xuan went to the Great Zhuang Hall for a grand military review, ordered Ren Zhong to array one hundred thousand foot and horse at Xuanwu Lake, and Chen Jing to lead five hundred tower ships onto the Yangzi at Guazhou; Emperor Xuan mounted the Xuanwu Gate tower [5] and feasted his ministers as they watched.

s0090.literal: He then visited the Leyou Garden and set a music gathering.
s0090.idiomatic: He then went to the Leyou Garden for a concert.

s0091.literal: He again visited the Great Zhuang Hall, gathered the armies, and returned after displaying their strength.
s0091.idiomatic: He returned to the Great Zhuang Hall, mustered the troops, and marched back in review.

s0092.literal: At that time Fangtai should have attended; he memorialized that his birth mother was ill and did not go; instead he went with twenty outlaws such as Yang Zhongqi in plain dress among the people and violated men's wives, and was arrested by the province.
s0092.idiomatic: Fangtai should have attended but pleaded his mother's illness; instead he went with twenty desperadoes including Yang Zhongqi in disguise among the people and raped women, and was seized by the provincial authorities.

s0093.literal: He also led men with weapons to resist, wounding the guards, and the responsible offices memorialized against him.
s0093.idiomatic: He also led armed men to resist and wounded the guards; the authorities reported him.

s0094.literal: The emperor was greatly angered and sent Fangtai to prison.
s0094.idiomatic: The emperor was furious and had Fangtai thrown into prison.

s0095.literal: Fangtai at first confessed only to the licentious conduct and did not confess to resisting the guards; the emperor said that if he did not confess they would use torture, and Fangtai then threw himself on the roster and confessed fully.
s0095.idiomatic: At first Fangtai admitted only the sexual crimes, not resisting the guards; the emperor said refusal would bring torture, and Fangtai then confessed everything on the record.

s0096.literal: Editorial footnote marker 6. Thereupon the acting censor-in-chief Xu Junfu memorialized, saying: "Your servant has heard that the heart of a king does not let the net leak to favor things, and the root of supreme order does not bend the law to extend kindness.
s0096.idiomatic: Editorial footnote marker 6. The acting censor-in-chief Xu Junfu then memorialized: "I have heard that a ruler's heart does not let offenders slip through the net for private favor, and that supreme order does not bend the law to show mercy.

s0097.literal: We respectfully report that Chen Fangtai of the house of Chen, though distant in the clan, has the fortune of kinship by marriage; in impeachment he has no achievement, and in joint governance he has scarce merit.
s0097.idiomatic: We report that Chen Fangtai, though a distant kinsman, enjoys the tie of marriage kin; as an inspector he has done nothing, and in office he has achieved little.

s0098.literal: The sage ruler, in great mercy, allowed him to repent the past and permitted his employment; the palace gates entrusted him with urgent duty, and he was charged with guarding the night watch.
s0098.idiomatic: Your Majesty in mercy let him repent and employed him again; the palace trusted him with urgent duty and made him hold the night watch.

s0099.literal: How could there be, when the golden gate opens at dawn and the jade carriage sets out at daybreak, a hundred offices racing and a thousand squadrons galloping—yet he fears the toil of this winged escort and recklessly raises a morning-and-evening plea?
s0099.idiomatic: When the palace gates open at dawn and the imperial carriage sets out, with a hundred offices rushing and a thousand guards riding, how could he shirk escort duty and falsely plead illness morning and night?

s0100.literal: Instead he turned his splendid cap toward the Qi River and his bright robes toward the mulberry grove—the fault of a subject, none greater than this; he ought follow the frost record and be permitted placement
